title: A cafaye service's declaration of its own account scoping
description: What a service publishes about the account boundary it enforces: the entry points that reach another account's data, the line at which each one is scoped, the test that proves it, and what the DATABASE does about it. One file per service, at its repository root, named tenancy.yml. It is here rather than in each repository because a rule that is not in schemas/ is not a cafaye rule, and because a boundary that is only discoverable by reading every query by hand is not a declaration at all. Checked by harness/tenancy_check.py; see docs/tenancy.md for why this file exists instead of a grep, for the three-way denial shape every entry point must prove, and for the ledger of Supabase's database advisor this file's `rls` block adapts.

version.description: The format version, a const rather than an absent field, so a declaration written for a later dialect cannot be read by an earlier reader without saying so.

service.description: Which service this declares, kebab-case. Deliberately NOT checked against the directory name, for the reason schemas/gate.schema.json's `name` is not: a git worktree's directory is not the repository's name, and a check that fires on `darkroom-worker-darkroom-10` is a check everybody learns to ignore. What it IS checked against is this service's own `cafaye.yml`, when the repository has one.

accountScoped.description: Whether this service scopes anything by account at all. Required, and a boolean, because the honest answer for a service that holds no customer data is `false` and it has to be able to say so — a service that is silent about its boundary is indistinguishable from a service that forgot, and only one of those is safe to ship. `false` is not an escape hatch: it is `tenancy.honest-zero`, a FAILURE, the moment a single account-scoped statement appears in the declared sources. `parkor` and `kit` are the fleet's two real zeros and they are zeros by construction rather than by omission.

entryPoints.description: The declared enumeration: every route, query, repository method or worker that reads or writes another account's data. DECLARED, NEVER INFERRED — see docs/tenancy.md for the measurement that decided it. `maxItems: 0` is legal only when `accountScoped` is false, so a service that genuinely has no account boundary can say so with an empty list instead of omitting itself. The other half of that rule is here too: `accountScoped: true` with an empty list is refused, because a service that says it scopes by account and then declares no way it does is the same omission wearing a declaration.

allOf.description: The second conditional, and it is the same argument as the first. A service whose database enforces nothing for it — which is every service in this fleet today, and is a legitimate and common design — has to be able to SAY that with an empty `rls.tables` rather than leave the block out, because a block nobody wrote and a block that says `false` are the same file to a reader who has not been told which one they are looking at. And `databaseEnforced: true` with no table in it is the database half of `accountScoped: true` with no entry point: the omission wearing a declaration, refused.

scope.description: What 'scoped by account' means in THIS service: the key, and the paths the checker is allowed to read looking for it. Both are required. A declaration that names the key but not the paths leaves the checker reading the whole tree, and a checker that reads the whole tree is a checker whose answer depends on whether `node_modules` is installed.

key.description: The tenancy column or parameter this service scopes by — `account_id` for SQL services, and whatever the service actually calls it otherwise. The checker searches for this and not for `tenant_id` or `org_id`, because the fleet has three vocabularies already (D7) and a checker that guesses which one a service uses is guessing at the boundary rather than at the data. A key that finds nothing in the declared sources is `tenancy.scope-key-unused`, a WARNING — the tool cannot prove a key is unused, but a misspelled key is worth saying out loud.

sources.description: Repository-relative paths the checker reads looking for account-scoped access. Directories are walked; a file is read as itself. At least one, because a checker told to look at nothing is a checker that cannot fail. Paths may not leave the repository, and they are resolved INSIDE it — this file reads a checkout and never fetches one.

nonRowSites.description: Sites where the declared tenancy key appears and is NOT a row scope — a verified token claim, a docstring, a vendored schema. Each names the file and line and carries the reason it is not a row scope, and the check still FAILS for any key-carrying site not named here: the field is how a service whose key appears only outside row scopes declares the honest zero in a language this checker cannot read, and it is not an escape hatch. A site the scanner attributed to a statement cannot be excused — a key this checker read in a select is a row scope by definition. Empty and optional; a service whose key appears nowhere does not need it.

rls.description: What this service's DATABASE does about the boundary, as opposed to what its application code does. This block is REQUIRED and it is not optional because of the reason `accountScoped` is required: a service whose database enforces nothing must be able to write `databaseEnforced: false` and an empty table list, and that has to be a different file from one where nobody thought about it. Cafaye is database-per-service, one database to a service, and the six services that hold customer rows today all scope in the application layer — so the honest answer for the whole fleet right now is `false`, and writing it down is what turns 'nobody asked' into 'nobody is claiming'. What the block REFUSES is the half-adopted state, which is the state this packet exists about: a migration that enables policies on a table this block does not list is `tenancy.rls-undeclared`, a FAILURE.

databaseEnforced.description: Whether Postgres row-level security is what holds the boundary for this service. A boolean and not an enum of mechanisms, because core declares exactly one mechanism and saying so in an enum with one entry would look like a vocabulary. `false` is the honest answer for a service whose repository layer scopes every statement — darkroom's shape — and `false` with a non-empty `tables` is refused below, because a service that says the database does nothing and then lists the tables it does something to is the same omission facing the other way. `false` is ALSO not a free pass: a policy anywhere in the declared sources is `tenancy.rls-undeclared`.

identity.description: The stable, zero-argument SQL function every policy reads the acting account from — `app.current_account_id()` in the shape cafaye uses. REQUIRED when `databaseEnforced` is true, because without it there is nothing to say a policy must be scoped by, and a policy that is scoped by nothing is `tenancy.rls-permissive`. It must end in `()` and take no arguments, for a reason that is not tidiness: the per-row rule (`tenancy.rls-per-row`) is about the call being wrapped in `(select …)` so Postgres evaluates it once per statement instead of once per row, and that only works on a call with no arguments, because a call with arguments cannot be hoisted. A `current_setting('app.account_id')` predicate is therefore not declarable here — it is the shape this field exists to steer away from, and `docs/tenancy.md` says why.

sources.description: Repository-relative paths holding this service's DDL — the migrations, and any other file the row-level-security posture is written in. A SEPARATE list from `scope.sources`, and the reason is that the two checks read genuinely different trees: a Go service's account-scoped statements are in `internal/` and its migrations are in `migrations/`, and one list containing both is a list that ends up naming the whole repository, which is the dependency-tree answer `harness/tenancy_findings.json`'s `notEnforced` entry names as this checker's sharpest limit. At least one, for the same reason `scope.sources` has at least one: a checker told to look at nothing is a checker that cannot fail. A declared path that is not there is `tenancy.scan-narrowed`, a WARNING, and the warning is the honest one — the scan read less than the declaration asked.

tables.description: Every table the DATABASE boundary covers, each with the policies that cover it and the bit that makes the bit mean anything. Empty exactly when `databaseEnforced` is false. There is no `maxItems: 0` escape in the other direction either: a table listed with `forced: false` does not validate, because `forced: false` IS the bug this packet is about and a format that can describe it is a format that will contain one.

publicRead.description: Tables that are deliberately public-readable, each with the policy that grants the read and the role it grants to. A claim with evidence, not a blanket exemption: the checker accepts a public SELECT policy on a declared table only when this list names that exact policy and the role the DDL binds it to, and a public read the DDL does not write is `tenancy.rls-public-read-absent`. SELECT-only — an always-true or role-less INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or ALL clause is still `tenancy.rls-permissive` under a public-read declaration.

rlsTable.description: One table, and the two facts about it that decide whether row-level security is doing anything at all.

table.description: The table, bare and lower snake_case, because that is the token the DDL scanner matches on and a comparison that had to normalise case would be a comparison with a judgement in it. Unqualified on purpose: cafaye is database-per-service with one schema the service owns, and a `schema.table` spelling here would let a declaration name a table in a schema this checker deliberately does not look at.

forced.description: That this table is set `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY`. `const: true`, and this is THE load-bearing constraint in the block, so it is worth saying why it is a const rather than a checked boolean. **Postgres does not apply row-level security to the table's OWNER unless the table is set FORCE.** A service that creates its tables in its own schema owns them, so a migration that writes `create policy`, then `alter table … enable row level security`, then stops has shipped a policy that is never evaluated by the role that matters — and nothing errors, nothing warns, and no query returns a wrong answer, because the policy is simply not consulted. Postgres documents this in the CREATE TABLE reference and NOT in the row-level-security guide, and Supabase's database advisor has no lint for it at all: `packages/pg-meta/src/sql/studio/advisor/lints.ts` reads `relforcerowsecurity` for the dashboard's table list and never judges it (measured, see docs/tenancy.md). So `forced: false` cannot be described here, and a table whose DDL does not carry the bit is `tenancy.rls-owner-bypass` — a FAILURE. The schema cannot see the DDL and the checker cannot see the schema, so each holds one half and `tenancy.rls-owner-bypass` is the place they meet.

policies.description: The policies on this table. At least one, because `enable row level security` with no policy denies every row to every role — including the one the service connects as, once the table is forced — and a deny-all table is indistinguishable from a correct one by anything that does not look at the third arm of the denial shape. A declared policy the DDL does not contain is `tenancy.rls-policy-absent`; a policy the DDL contains that is not declared is `tenancy.rls-undeclared`.

rlsPolicy.description: One policy: which commands it governs, who it governs them for, and the line the clause is on. Postgres's two denial mechanisms are different mechanisms and want different assertions, so which one is named here rather than left to the reader.

name.description: The policy's name as written in the DDL, because the whole point of naming it is that the checker can find THAT policy in THAT `create policy` rather than being satisfied by any policy on the table. A policy that stops existing is `tenancy.rls-policy-absent`.

command.description: What the policy governs, spelled the way the DDL spells it. `all` is Postgres's default when a policy omits `for`, and it is here rather than refused because it is legal and common. `insert` is legal HERE and is deliberately absent from `entryPoints[].operation`, and the two absences are not the same rule: an entry point is a statement that reaches an account's EXISTING row, and an insert creates one rather than reaching one, so it cannot be a cross-tenant leak. A policy's `for insert` is a constraint on a row the caller is creating, and `with check (account_id = …)` is what stops a caller stamping somebody else's account onto a new row — a different question about the same boundary, asked by a different piece of Postgres.

clause.description: Which of the two clauses denies the access, and it is derived from `command` rather than chosen. `USING` filters the rows a command may SEE, so a denied statement matches zero rows and **raises nothing**; `WITH CHECK` is evaluated against the row a command is about to write, and a violation **raises 42501**. That difference is not trivia: it decides whether the denial test asserts an empty result or an exception, and asserting an exception where the policy filters the row out is asserting a privilege failure and passing for the wrong reason. `update` and `all` may carry either, so no arm of that conditional is written for them.

roles.description: The roles the policy applies to, which is Postgres's `to` clause, and it is REQUIRED and named because a policy with no `to` clause applies to `PUBLIC` — every role, including the migration role and every role this service adds later. A `public` entry is refused by the `not` below rather than merely discouraged, for the same reason `negative.asserts` is a `const`: in a database with one named runtime role, a policy that silently applies to everything is a boundary nobody wrote. Naming the roles is also how the checker can tell a policy that is scoped to the runtime role from one scoped to a role with `BYPASSRLS`, which is `tenancy.rls-role-bypass`.

constrained.description: The line the clause is written on, and it must carry the identity named in `rls.identity` — wrapped in `(select …)`, not bare. The file and the line are both checked on disk for the reason `enforced.file` and `enforced.line` are: a declaration that points at nothing reads as a boundary somebody looked at, and this one is worse, because a policy clause that has moved is a policy nobody is reading.

publicRead.description: One table that is deliberately public-readable, and the two facts that make it a claim rather than an exemption: the policy that grants the read, and the role that read is granted to. The checker accepts a public SELECT policy on a declared table only when this list names that exact policy and a role the DDL binds it to — a public read nobody declares is still `tenancy.rls-permissive`, and a public read the DDL does not write is `tenancy.rls-public-read-absent`. SELECT-only: an always-true or role-less INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE or ALL clause is still `tenancy.rls-permissive` under a public-read declaration. The named policy must ALSO be declared in `rls.tables[].policies`, because a policy in the migrations and not in `rls.tables` is `tenancy.rls-undeclared` — this list is the evidence that the policy is a deliberate public read, not a replacement for declaring it.

table.description: The table that is deliberately public-readable. Bare and lower snake_case, the same spelling `rls.tables[].table` carries, because the checker matches the public-read claim against the declared table and the DDL on that token — a comparison that had to normalise case would be a comparison with a judgement in it.

policy.description: The policy that grants the public read, spelled the way the DDL spells it. The whole point of naming it is that the checker can find THAT policy in THAT `create policy` and compare the role the DDL binds it to against the role named here — a bare `publicRead: true` with no named policy is the thing this field exists to avoid.

role.description: The role the public read is granted to — one role, the policy's `to` clause named. A policy with no `to` clause applies to PUBLIC, which is every role including the migration role and every role this service adds later, and that is not a public-read tier: it is the absence of a boundary. The checker compares this against the roles the DDL binds, so a declaration naming a role the policy does not grant to is `tenancy.rls-public-read-absent`.

located.description: A repository-relative file and a 1-indexed line in it. Both are checked on disk, and neither may leave the repository.

nonRowSite.description: One place the tenancy key appears and is not a row scope. `file` and `line` are the site, checked on disk the way `located` checks them; `reason` is why this is not a row scope, and it is required because a site named with no reason is the 'I cannot see this' this field exists to replace. The checker excuses a scanned site only when its file and line match one of these exactly, and only when the scanner could not attribute that line to a statement — so the field vouches for what the declaration can see and never for what the scanner could read.

reason.description: Why this site is not a row scope — 'a verified token claim, read off the caller', 'a docstring describing the verification', 'core's vendored telemetry schema'. A sentence, not a label: the reader who has to decide whether to trust the zero is a human, and the reason is what they read.

entryPoint.description: One way this service reaches another account's data, and the three things that make the declaration a contract rather than a summary: where the scoping happens, and the test that proves it.

id.description: What this entry point is called, kebab-case and unique across the list. Unique because `uniqueItems` compares whole objects, and two entry points with different `line` values are two objects; the id is what a reader, a test and a failure message all name.

operation.description:
What it does to another account's row: `select`, `update` or `delete` — the three the checker's scanner recognises, and the three against which the enumeration is closed in BOTH directions (a site it finds that nobody declared, and a declaration whose site it can no longer find). `call` is for a repository method, a worker or a route whose scoping is enforced above the statement; closure cannot be checked against it, and the checker says so out loud as `tenancy.enumeration-partial` rather than quietly counting it as covered.

`insert` is deliberately ABSENT, and the omission is the rule. An insert creates a row in the account the caller is already acting as; it cannot read, and cannot write, another account's row, so it is not a place a cross-tenant leak can happen. Adding it would mean a legal declaration whose `enforced.line` does not carry the tenancy key — the account is in the column list, not in a predicate — and an exception inside the contract is how the next exception gets added. A row-level-security policy's `for insert` is a different thing and `rls.policies[].command` does carry it; see that field for why the two lists differ rather than sharing a vocabulary.

subject.description: What it reaches: a table name, or the method or route that reaches it. Lower snake_case, because it is the identity the scanner matches on and a comparison that had to normalise case would be a comparison with a judgement in it. Line numbers do NOT participate: an entry point's identity is its subject and what it does, so a refactor that moves a query three lines down does not turn ten declarations red, while a refactor that drops its `and account_id = $2` does.

enforced.description: Where the boundary is drawn in the source. The file and the line are both required and both checked on disk: a declaration that points at nothing is worse than no declaration, because it reads as a boundary somebody looked at. The line is EXACT, and the drift that causes is the intended trade — see docs/tenancy.md §"why the line is a line".

mechanism.description: How the scoping is actually done here, from a closed vocabulary rather than prose. A prose field is a summary; this is a claim the checker can look at, because all four mechanisms have to put the tenancy key somewhere on the declared line — a predicate, a bind parameter, a method signature, or the point where the request's account is resolved onto the context every later read reads from.

binds.description: The parameter that carries the account, REQUIRED when `mechanism` is `bind-parameter` and forbidden otherwise. This is the field that catches the breakage a predicate check cannot: a query that still says `account_id = $2` while nothing passes `$2` any more is scoped on paper and unscoped in fact, which is `tenancy.bind-missing`.

file.description: Repository-relative path to the file the scoping is in. Checked on disk, and `tenancy.location-missing` is a failure when it is not there.

line.description: The 1-indexed line the scoping is enforced on. Must be a line that exists — `tenancy.line-missing` past the end of the file — and must carry the tenancy key in one of its three fleet spellings (`account_id`, `accountId`, `account-id`), which is `tenancy.scope-lost` when it does not.

negative.description:
THE THREE-WAY DENIAL SHAPE, and it is the load-bearing block in this file. The question a boundary has to answer is not "does an unauthenticated request fail" — that is satisfied by a table with no policy at all, by a table with no predicate at all, and by a service whose database is switched off, which is the BUG rather than the fix. The question is three questions, and `cases` is exactly three of them: `no-identity` reads zero rows, `other-account` — a VALID credential belonging to a different account — reads zero rows, and `own-account` **sees its own rows**.

The third arm is the one that carries the information, and it is why `asserts` is per-case rather than one value for the block: a service may not answer it with an absent-shaped result, because "every call returns nothing" satisfies both negative arms and describes a service that cannot serve its own customer. `own-account` is `const: present`, the two denial arms are `const: absent`, and a `refusal` is legal nowhere in this block — cross-tenant access is answered as NONEXISTENCE (D33), because a `403` confirms the id exists.

`cases` replaced a single `expects`/`file`/`line` triple, and the reason is in `docs/tenancy.md` under the three-way heading: with one assertion the shape looked covered while the arm with all the information in it was the one nobody wrote.

asserts.description: `absent`, and only `absent`. The block's own answer to cross-tenant access, which the two denial cases restate per arm and the third case is the exception to: that one asserts a row is PRESENT. Kept at this level as well as per case because it is the vocabulary anchor the whole file is built on, and because a reader who has read one `const` has read the rule.

cases.description: Exactly three, in the order above. `minItems` and `maxItems` are both 3 rather than `minItems: 3` alone, because an open upper bound is how a fourth case gets added — and a fourth case would be a case about something this format has no opinion on, which is how an exception becomes a convention.

id.description: Which of the three identities is acting. A closed vocabulary, because the whole claim is that there are three and the value of saying so is destroyed by a fourth.

asserts.description: What the assertion concludes. `absent` for the two denial arms, `present` for the third, and derived from `id` below rather than chosen.

expects.description:
The token the checker looks for ON the declared line, and what it means depends on `asserts`. For an `absent` arm it is the language's own spelling of nothing: `nil`, `None`, `NotFound`, `ErrNotFound`, `not_found`, or the empty list as the language writes it (`[]`). For a write it is the assertion's own name where the language has no absent value to return (`rows_affected_zero`, `assert_unchanged`): what is being asserted is that the other account's row came back as it was, and an empty list would be a lie about a row that exists. For the `present` arm it is the column or field the assertion reads off the row that came back — `checksum`, `status` — because the third arm has to show the row's OWN value, not merely that a call did not raise; `lives_ok` passes when the write matched zero rows, which is the exact failure the third arm exists to catch. And it is refused to be an absent spelling here: `tenancy.positive-control-refused` is a FAILURE when the third arm's token is one the language uses for nothing.

WHAT IT MAY NOT BE is the other half of this field, and it is why the pattern is a pattern rather than an enum of six languages' spellings. Postgres denies a cross-tenant access three ways and only two of them raise: a missing grant and a `with check` violation both raise `42501`, while a `using` clause filtering the row out raises NOTHING and matches zero rows. So `select`, `update` and `delete` — the three operations denied by `using` — may not name a token that asserts a raise, which is `tenancy.denial-shape`; `select`, `update` and `delete` may not name a token that asserts only that nothing was raised (`lives_ok`, `does_not_raise`, …), for the reason above; and the two denial arms of a write may not name an absent spelling at all, which is `tenancy.denial-unpaired` — a write's zero row count is also what a write that found nothing to do returns, so only a read of the row it was aimed at tells a refusal from a no-op. Those three vocabularies live in `harness/tenancy_check.py` rather than here, because they are facts about the SERVICE's test file and no JSON Schema can ask whether a line in another language contains `assert_raises`.

file.description: Repository-relative path to the test file carrying the assertion. A service that cannot name the test does not have one; that is `tenancy.denial-missing`, and it is a failure rather than a warning because the assertion is not optional evidence, it is the deliverable.

line.description: The 1-indexed line carrying the assertion, and it must carry `expects`. Weakening the assertion from absent to forbidden is `tenancy.denial-missing` when the declaration is left alone and `tenancy.denial-refuses` when it is updated to match. Both directions are a red, which is the point.
